## Previously · Logarithms as exponents {#fgt3-previously .trig-lesson .log-lesson}

A logarithm tells us the **exponent**.

$$\log_{10}x=u\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=10^u,\qquad x>0$$

::: {.log-recap}

| Exponential form | Logarithmic form |
|---|---|
| $10^3=1000$ | $\log_{10}1000=3$ |
| $10^0=1$ | $\log_{10}1=0$ |
| $10^{-3}=0.001$ | $\log_{10}0.001=-3$ |

:::

::: {.takeaway}
$\log_{10}A-\log_{10}B=\log_{10}\!\left(\dfrac{A}{B}\right)$, for $A,B>0$.
:::

::: notes

Check the direction of the conversion and the role of a negative exponent. A negative logarithm is possible because its input can be a positive number less than 1; it does not mean taking the logarithm of a negative number. Recall the quotient law so that comparisons of scale readings can later be combined into one logarithm. Allow about 2 minutes.

:::
